'''Roberto Car''' (born 3 January 1947 in [[Trieste]]) is an Italian [[physicist]] and the Ralph W. Dornte *31 Professor in Chemistry at [[Princeton University]], where he is also a faculty member in the Princeton Institute for the Science and Technology of Materials.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Roberto Car {{!}} Princeton University Department of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/car|access-date=2020-06-15|website=chemistry.princeton.edu|archive-date=2020-06-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200616100943/https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/car|url-status=dead}}</ref> He researches the simulation of [[molecular dynamics]] phenomena.

==Life==
Car studied [[physics]] and attained a doctorate in 1971 in nuclear technology at the [[Politecnico di Milano]]. He was a postdoc at the [[University of Milan]] from 1973 to 1974, an assistant at the [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]] (EPFL) from 1977 to 1981, employed at the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] of [[international Business Machine|IBM]] from 1981 to 1983, associate professor for physics at [[SISSA]] in [[Trieste]] (in 1990/91 as full professor) from 1984 to 1990, and professor for physics at the [[University of Geneva]] (and director of the IRRMA of EPFL) from 1991 to 1999.

He is a professor in the Theory Department of the Fritz Haber Institute of the [[Max Planck Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fhi-berlin.mpg.de/th/cms/index.php?option=com_wrapper&Itemid=226 |title=Theory Department of the FHI - Theory Department - Prof. Dr. Roberto Car |publisher=Fhi-berlin.mpg.de |date= |accessdate=2010-07-31}}</ref>

He is a member of the Italian Scientists and Scholars in North America Foundation.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.issnaf.org/web/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=19&Itemid=27 |title=About Us: Who We Are |publisher=Issnaf.org |date= |accessdate=2010-07-31 |archive-date=2010-12-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101215230921/http://issnaf.org/web/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=19&Itemid=27 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Awards==
In 2009 he shared the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] with [[Michele Parrinello]] for their development of the ''ab initio'' molecular dynamics simulation method. The method combines the quantum mechanical [[density functional theory]] for calculation of electronic structure with methods of molecular dynamics for the simulation of classical ("Newtonian") atomic movements. They call their procedure ''ab initio molecular dynamics ''; it is also well known as the [[Car–Parrinello method]]. The procedure was jointly developed by both men in 1985,<ref>'' Unified Approach for Molecular Dynamics and Density Functional Theory '', Physical Review Letters, Vol.55, 1985, pp.2471-4, [https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2471 Abstract]</ref> while working at [[SISSA]] in Trieste. Their procedure has found various applications in solid-state physics, biochemistry, chemical physics, and [[materials science]].

In 1990 he received the Hewlett-Packard prize of the [[European Physical Society]], in 1995 the Rahman Prize of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.researchcrossroads.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=49&Itemid=55&user_id=806277 |title=Roberto Car &#124; Princeton University &#124; ResearchCrossroads Profile |publisher=Researchcrossroads.org |date= |accessdate=2010-07-31}}</ref> where he is a Fellow, and in 2009 with Parinello the [[Sidney Fernbach Award]] of the [[IEEE]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.computer.org/portal/web/pressroom/2009/fernbach |title=Car and Parrinello Named 2009 Fernbach Winners |publisher=Computer.org |date=2009-10-15 |accessdate=2010-07-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=|url=http://www.nanowerk.com/news/newsid=13191.php |title=Roberto Car, Michele Parrinello win Computer Society's Fernbach Award |publisher=Nanowerk.com |date=2009-10-22 |accessdate=2010-07-31}}</ref> In 2008, he received the Humboldt Foundation Research Award for senior US scientists. In 2007, a birthday symposium was held at ICTP.<ref>[http://users.ictp.it/~cm/Car_program_8.pdf "Roberto Car 60th Birthday Symposium"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304025649/http://users.ictp.it/~cm/Car_program_8.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }}, accessdate July 31, 2010</ref> He received the [[Aneesur Rahman]] prize in computational physics. The [[Aneesur Rahman Prize]] is the highest honor given by the [[American Physical Society]] for work in [[computational physics]]. In 2020 he was awarded the [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)]] in Chemistry.<ref>[https://www.fi.edu/awards Benjamin Franklin Medal 2020]</ref>

In 2016 he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-3-2016-NAS-Election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506052951/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-3-2016-NAS-Election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 6, 2016|title=National Academy of Sciences Members and Foreign Associates Elected|department=News from the National Academy of Sciences|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|date=May 3, 2016|accessdate=2016-05-14}}.</ref> In the same year he was awarded the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Award in Theoretical Chemistry.
